title: Absolute and Relational Space and Motion: Post-Newtonian Theories

summaries.example: Imagine a spinning bucket of water. The water may move compared with the bucket, but the important question is what causes the water to push outward. Mach asked whether the answer could involve the water’s motion compared with all the stars and other matter in the universe, rather than an invisible absolute space.
summaries.summary: This entry explores a long-running question: what is motion, and does it need an absolute space as a background? Ernst Mach challenged Newton’s absolute space and suggested that motion and inertia might depend on relationships among all the material things in the universe. The entry distinguishes a modest view, called Mach-lite, from a stronger Mach-heavy view. It then examines Einstein’s special and general relativity, modern shape dynamics, and the dynamical approach to spacetime. These theories reduce or reinterpret some absolute features, but none simply ends every philosophical disagreement. The main lesson is that physics can describe motion in different ways, and each way raises questions about what is most basic: space, matter, relations, or laws of motion.
key_ideas: Philosophers and physicists have disagreed about whether space and motion are real things on their own or depend on relationships between objects.
Ernst Mach criticized Newton’s idea of absolute space because it could not be directly observed.
Mach-lite keeps much of Newton’s mechanics but uses the distant stars as a practical reference.
Mach-heavy asks for a deeper theory in which the matter in the universe helps explain inertia and rotation.
Einstein’s theories remove absolute velocity, but general relativity does not completely settle whether all motion is relative.
Shape dynamics is a modern attempt to describe the universe using relations such as shapes, angles, and changes rather than absolute positions and sizes.
summaries.why_it_matters: The question affects how we understand spinning, falling, time, gravity, and even what counts as a real part of nature. It also shows that science is not only about measuring things. Scientists and philosophers ask what the measurements mean and which ideas are needed to explain them.

important_terms.definition: The idea that motion can be described only through relationships between objects, such as one object changing position compared with another.
The view that space, motion, or some features of motion exist independently of relationships between objects.
A suggested standard of motion in which an object keeps moving steadily unless a force changes its motion.
A proposal inspired by Mach that the motion of matter throughout the universe helps determine effects such as inertia and rotation.

questions_to_think_about: If everything in the universe moved together, how could we tell that it moved?
Does a spinning object need space itself as a reference, or could it refer only to other matter?
Why might scientists want a theory that uses fewer invisible ingredients?
Can a useful description leave out something that might still be real?

summaries.example: Consider a spacecraft far from planets. In Newtonian physics, if it accelerates, one explanation is that it is accelerating relative to absolute space. Einstein’s equivalence principle offers another description: the spacecraft could be treated as at rest in a uniform gravitational field. This does not by itself prove that all acceleration is merely relative. General relativity permits models, including nearly empty ones, in which spacetime structure remains even when matter is absent. That is why the theory has Mach-friendly features without fully realizing Mach-heavy relationism.
summaries.summary: The entry examines post-Newtonian attempts to clarify whether space and motion are absolute or relational. Mach’s critique of Newton motivates two positions. Mach-lite rejects absolute space as an unnecessary metaphysical addition while retaining a practical reference based on the distant stars. Mach-heavy demands more: inertial effects should arise from the relative distribution and motion of all matter, perhaps with new gravitational effects. Einstein’s special relativity genuinely removes absolute velocity and time, but it retains a distinction between inertial and accelerated motion. General relativity goes further: its metric both represents spacetime geometry and encodes gravity, and in some models matter strongly determines inertial structure. Yet the theory also permits empty spacetime and isolated rotating objects, so it does not universally realize Einstein’s Machian hopes. Shape dynamics attempts to remove absolute position, scale, and temporal structure through reduced configuration spaces and best matching. The dynamical approach instead asks whether spacetime geometry should be understood through symmetries and behavior of matter. The entry concludes that “absolute” and “relative” do not have one perfectly stable meaning across the history of physics, and that several different philosophical questions are often grouped under those labels.
key_ideas: Mach’s criticism of Newton targets the unobservable status of absolute space, but his writings support both a modest and a strong interpretation.
Mach-lite can reproduce ordinary Newtonian predictions when the distant stars provide a nearly fixed reference, but it gives less guidance in unusual cosmological situations.
Mach-heavy seeks to derive inertial effects from relations involving all matter. Barbour-Bertotti theories and shape dynamics are attempts to implement this goal.

Special relativity removes absolute velocity and absolute time, yet it still distinguishes inertial from accelerated motion. Spacetime interval relations can encode acceleration, but this does not automatically eliminate absolute acceleration.

General relativity has no fixed background spacetime in its standard formulation, and its metric is partly linked to matter and energy. Nevertheless, it allows vacuum and isolated rotating solutions, so it does not satisfy Mach-heavy in every model.

The dynamical approach changes the explanatory direction: instead of spacetime explaining the symmetries of matter’s laws, the laws and their symmetries may explain the relevant spacetime structure. This debate is related to, but not identical with, relationism versus substantivalism.
summaries.why_it_matters: These debates concern the interpretation of successful physical theories, not merely word choices. They ask whether spacetime is an independent entity, a structure determined by matter, or a useful representation of patterns in dynamical laws. The answers influence how we understand gravity, inertia, general relativity, and attempts to develop new theories such as shape dynamics or quantum gravity.

important_terms.definition: The view that motion is fundamentally describable through relations among bodies or events, rather than through comparison with an independent absolute space.
The view that space or spacetime has structure, and perhaps reality, that is not fully grounded in relations among material bodies.
The Newtonian idea of a fixed spatial background that provides an independent standard for position, velocity, and acceleration.
Mach’s stronger proposal that inertial effects should be determined by the distribution and relative motions of massive bodies throughout the universe.
A weaker Mach-inspired strategy that removes absolute space from practical Newtonian mechanics while using the frame of the distant stars as a standard.
The principle that, locally, being in a uniformly accelerating rocket can resemble being at rest in a uniform gravitational field.
A modern research program that attempts to formulate dynamics using relational shapes, while treating absolute position, scale, and sometimes time as dispensable.
The view that spacetime structure is explained by, or reduced to, regular patterns and symmetries in the laws governing matter.

questions_to_think_about: Does a one-to-one match between motion and spacetime relations show that motion has been reduced to relations, or only that the two descriptions correlate?
Why is Mach-lite attractive for empiricists but less satisfying to philosophers who expect laws to cover every possible universe?
If general relativity allows empty spacetime, what does that imply for the claim that matter creates all inertial structure?
Should a theory prefer fewer absolute quantities even if competing theories make the same predictions?
Can the symmetries of dynamical laws explain spacetime structure without presupposing some spacetime structure already?

summaries.example: Suppose you are inside a spaceship with no windows. You feel pushed toward the floor. One explanation says the ship is accelerating through absolute space. Another says you are at rest in a gravitational field filling the ship. Einstein’s equivalence principle shows why these descriptions can look alike in a small region. But general relativity still allows an empty spacetime background and a single rotating object, so it does not make every motion depend completely on surrounding matter.
summaries.summary: This entry studies contemporary versions of the debate over absolute and relational space and motion. Ernst Mach’s criticism of Newton’s absolute space can be read in two ways. Mach-lite keeps Newtonian mechanics but replaces absolute space with a reference connected to the distant stars. Mach-heavy seeks a new mechanics in which inertial effects arise from relations among all massive bodies. Einstein’s special relativity removes absolute velocity and changes the treatment of space and time, but it does not remove the difference between inertial and accelerated motion. General relativity offers a more complicated picture. Its spacetime metric is connected with gravity and is partly shaped by matter and energy; some models display effects close to Mach’s proposal. Yet the theory also permits empty spacetime and isolated rotating systems, which means that Mach-heavy is not satisfied throughout the theory. Shape dynamics tries to build physics from relational configurations, removing certain absolute quantities through mathematical identification and best matching. The dynamical approach takes a different route, arguing that spacetime structure may be explained by the symmetries of matter’s laws. The entry emphasizes that the absolute-relative debate contains several related but distinct philosophical problems.
key_ideas: The entry separates several questions that are often mixed together: whether some motions are privileged, whether privileged motion can be defined through relations, and whether spacetime is an entity in its own right.
Mach-lite is close to ordinary Newtonian practice, but it does not clearly say what happens in universes without nearly fixed stars.
Mach-heavy would make inertia depend on the universe’s matter. It is a stronger and more ambitious form of relationism.
Special relativity removes a preferred state of uniform velocity, but it still gives a physical distinction between inertial and accelerated motion.
General relativity combines gravity with spacetime geometry and has both Mach-friendly and anti-Machian models.
Shape dynamics uses mathematical spaces of possible configurations and procedures such as best matching to identify descriptions that differ only by overall shifts, rotations, or changes of scale.
summaries.why_it_matters: Understanding these options helps explain why the same physical theory can support different philosophical interpretations. The issues reach from everyday questions about spinning and acceleration to deep questions about gravity, geometry, scientific explanation, and what a physical theory should regard as fundamental.

important_terms.definition: The position that motion is meaningful only through relationships among objects or events.
The position that space or spacetime can provide a standard for motion that does not depend entirely on matter.
Mach’s weaker proposal: use the distant stars as a practical frame instead of adding an unobservable absolute space.
Mach’s stronger proposal: inertia and related effects should be explained by the relative motion and distribution of all massive bodies.
A frame of reference in which a freely moving body follows the simple motion described by the laws of inertia.
The idea that a uniformly accelerating spaceship can locally produce effects like standing in a uniform gravitational field.
A theory-building program that describes physical histories using relational shapes and attempts to remove absolute position, size, and time.
An approach claiming that spacetime structure may be explained by the laws governing matter and by those laws’ symmetries.

questions_to_think_about: Is using the distant stars as a reference enough to eliminate absolute space, or does it merely replace one standard with another?
Why might acceleration be harder to treat as purely relative than velocity?
Does the existence of vacuum solutions in general relativity count against Mach-heavy relationism?
What might be gained by treating spacetime structure as a result of laws rather than as an independent background?
Are two theories philosophically equivalent if they make similar predictions but describe what is real differently?
